title: Chapter 8 — The Pulpit
paragraphs: I hadn't been seated long before a man of impressive, weathered strength entered. The moment the storm-battered door swung open to admit him, every eye in the congregation turned toward him, confirming that this fine old man was the chaplain. Yes, it was the famous Father Mapple — so called by the whalemen, among whom he was a great favorite. He'd been a sailor and harpooneer in his youth but had devoted his life to the ministry for many years. At the time I write of, Father Mapple was in the hardy winter of a healthy old age — the kind that seems to merge into a second blooming youth, for among the crevices of his wrinkles shone mild gleams of a newly developing vitality, like spring green peeping out beneath February's snow. Anyone seeing Father Mapple for the first time couldn't help being fascinated, because his manner carried certain clerical quirks clearly rooted in his adventurous life at sea. When he entered, I noticed he carried no umbrella and certainly hadn't arrived by carriage — his oilskin hat was streaming with melting sleet, and his heavy pilot jacket seemed ready to drag him to the floor under the weight of water it had absorbed. But hat, coat, and overshoes were removed one by one and hung in a little corner space. Then, wearing a decent suit, he quietly approached the pulpit.

Like most old-fashioned pulpits, it was very high, and since a regular staircase would have taken up too much of the chapel's already small floor space, the architect — apparently acting on Father Mapple's suggestion — had built the pulpit without stairs, using instead a perpendicular side ladder, like those used to board a ship from a boat at sea. A whaling captain's wife had provided a handsome pair of red woolen hand-ropes for this ladder, which itself was neatly made and stained mahogany. The whole setup, considering what kind of chapel this was, seemed in perfectly good taste. Pausing at the foot of the ladder and grasping the ornamental knobs of the hand-ropes, Father Mapple cast a look upward, then with a truly sailor-like but still reverent agility, hand over hand, climbed the steps as if ascending the mainmast of his vessel.

The vertical sides of this ladder were cloth-covered rope, with only the rungs made of wood, so every step had a joint. At first glance, it struck me that these joints, however practical on a ship, seemed unnecessary here. I wasn't prepared for what came next: Father Mapple, having reached the top, slowly turned around, leaned over the pulpit, and deliberately pulled the ladder up behind him, step by step, until the whole thing was deposited inside — leaving him impregnable in his little Quebec.

I puzzled over this for some time. Father Mapple had such a wide reputation for sincerity and holiness that I couldn't suspect him of seeking attention through stage tricks. No, I thought, there must be a serious reason for this. And it must symbolize something unseen. Could it be that by physically isolating himself, he was signifying a spiritual withdrawal from all worldly ties and connections? Yes — for replenished with the bread and wine of God's word, this pulpit becomes, for the faithful man of God, a self-contained fortress — a lofty stronghold with a perpetual spring of water within its walls.

But the side ladder wasn't the only feature borrowed from the chaplain's seafaring days. Between the marble memorial tablets on either side of the pulpit, the back wall displayed a large painting of a brave ship battling a terrible storm off a rocky lee shore of black cliffs and white breakers. But high above the flying spray and dark rolling clouds floated a little island of sunlight, from which beamed an angel's face. This bright face cast a distinct spot of radiance on the ship's tossing deck, like the silver plate set into the Victory's planking where Nelson fell. 'Ah, noble ship,' the angel seemed to say, 'beat on, noble ship, and hold a steady helm; for the sun is breaking through, the clouds are rolling away — clear blue sky lies ahead.'

The pulpit itself also carried traces of the same sea-inspiration. Its paneled front was shaped like a ship's bluff bow, and the Holy Bible rested on a projecting piece of scrollwork fashioned after a ship's figurehead.

What could be more fitting? For the pulpit is the earth's foremost part; everything else follows in its wake. The pulpit leads the world. From there, the storm of God's swift wrath is first spotted, and the bow must bear the earliest blow. From there, the God of fair winds and foul is first called upon. Yes, the world is a ship on an outward voyage, not yet complete; and the pulpit is its prow.
